title: The Illusion of Understanding: How Middle-Schoolers Fail to Regulate Inquiry with ChatGPT in a Science Task
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether middle-school students can use ChatGPT in ways that support meaningful science learning. The authors focus on a core problem in generative AI-supported learning: students may over-rely on the tool, accept vague or low-quality answers, and fail to regulate their inquiry even when they believe they understand the content.

The study investigates three linked skills during science investigation tasks: judging whether a suggested prompt is efficient, evaluating the quality of ChatGPT’s answers, and deciding whether to ask follow-up questions or stop. The activity used six science problems validated for middle-school curriculum relevance. Students were shown either efficient or inefficient suggested prompts, could also write their own prompts, and interacted with ChatGPT 3.5 while rating every response they received. Researchers also measured AI attitudes, prior domain knowledge, and metacognitive skills.

Participants were 63 French middle-school students aged 14–15 from four schools in Nouvelle-Aquitaine, France. The findings showed that students generally struggled to distinguish efficient from inefficient prompts and also had low sensitivity to whether AI answers were informative. Very few asked follow-up questions, even after receiving weak answers. Higher positive attitudes toward AI and greater self-reported prior knowledge were associated with poorer evaluation of prompts and answers, while metacognitive regulation predicted better prompt discrimination. The authors conclude that science education needs AI literacy interventions that emphasize metacognitive regulation, skepticism, and understanding the difference between high-level explanations and superficial information.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical observational study with a relatively small sample and no randomized comparison condition. It provides clear behavioral and correlational evidence, but credibility is limited by the single-group design and reliance on task-specific measures.
impact_tier_rationale: The observed learning outcome is modest and the interaction deficits are substantial, but the paper does not test an intervention designed to improve outcomes. Its main contribution is diagnostic rather than demonstrating a measurable positive educational impact.

interventions.use_case: middle-school science investigation tasks where students use ChatGPT 3.5 to ask questions, evaluate answers, and continue or terminate inquiry cycles

finding.finding_summary: Students used ChatGPT in six middle-school science investigation tasks (n=63), but conceptual understanding remained limited: the average correct final solution rate was Msuccess=0.51 (SD=0.25), and final responses were binary-coded for deep, accurate scientific explanations. Students often received useful high-level answers only when prompts were efficient, yet their weak prompt discrimination, poor answer evaluation, and low follow-up behavior constrained learning outcomes.
finding.measure: binary-coded final written explanations of scientific concepts; success rate across six science investigation tasks

finding.finding_summary: Students showed near-chance performance in several metacognitive interaction skills with GenAI: prompt discrimination sensitivity was Md′=0.19 (SD=0.8; t=1.77, p=0.08) and answer-evaluation sensitivity was Md′=0.07 (SD=1.2; t=-0.45, p=0.65). Follow-up regulation was rare, with only 14 of 63 students asking follow-up questions (22 total across six tasks), indicating weak metacognitive monitoring, critical evaluation, and persistence in the QA cycle.
finding.measure: signal-detection sensitivity for prompt and answer discrimination; frequency of follow-up questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports low-quality engagement with the AI-mediated inquiry process, including premature termination of QA cycles and over-reliance on AI responses. High prior confidence and positive AI attitudes were associated with poorer interaction quality, suggesting that perceived ease or trust reduced students’ willingness to persist and self-regulate during the task.
finding.measure: follow-up-question behavior; self-reported AI attitudes and prior knowledge confidence
